# The Fear of the Lord: Proverbs as Coherent Vision of Faith Formation

For many, the book of Proverbs is an ancient compendium of wisdom sayings: a collection of assorted, concise, and practical observations on living life well. Not a few read this portion of Scripture for the ease of its immediate application and real-world implementation. Succinct and compact, many of these wise sayings lodge themselves in one's mind as they directly connect (sometimes effortlessly) with shared human experience. It is true that a bulk of this inspired Scripture consists of pithy maxims relevant to a wide range of useful topics: self-control, marriage, friendship, speech, finances, business, neighborliness, oaths, and work. In this sense, Proverbs is accessible and adored because it profitably and profoundly addresses humanity's felt needs and pressing concerns. The collection of inspired wisdom is applicable in its breadth and profound in its depth, giving it a universal quality.

But Proverbs is much more than a topical index addressing miscellaneous subjects. The appeal of its immediate relevance to life interests is supported by its much deeper offerings. The broad range of thematic interests—expressions of wisdom—in Proverbs is supported by a sound substructure about the nature, value, and essence of wisdom. In this way, when Proverbs is viewed as a whole book—intentionally organized and arranged—it offers a holistic vision and integrated system for the life of faith. As a carefully designed book, Proverbs inspires us to faith formation in the fear of God. Taking note of the texture, emphasis, and structure of this biblical book will help us understand its portrayal of wisdom along with patterns and principles for faith development.

First, Proverbs offers a portrait of a godly life. Overarching its many topics is an urgent moral concern. True wisdom is not merely about living a successful life on the world's terms, but living a righteous life before the true and living God. Biblical wisdom offers a picture of a well-lived earthly existence in order to secure a God-given eternal inheritance. Alongside the common contrasts between wise and fools, simple and prudent, and youthful and learned are the moral contrasts between good and evil, righteous and wicked, and just and unjust. Solomon commends to us: the righteous life is the epitome of wise living. Proverbs is more interested in blessings that come from moral formation—conformity to the character of God—than about maximizing transient earthly benefits.

Second, Proverbs does not leave us in the dark about how moral formation occurs. Inasmuch as it offers insight into the content of wisdom, it also illuminates the path on how to become wise. In particular, Proverbs 1-9 serves this unique purpose. The bulk of these first nine chapters offer a series of lectures—appeals to Solomon's son(s)—on why he must obtain wisdom at all costs. In the course of making his earnest appeals, he elucidates how a simple youth can grow into a godly adult. Proverbs 1-9 not only serves as an introduction to the book—an initial appeal before the topical assortment of maxims—it also presents a theology of formation. In essence, Solomon's lectures to his son offer a biblical perspective on education: a spiritual pedagogy that helps God's people know how transformation, maturity, and growth take place. These principles help us know "how people change" in a way that serves our own personal growth, the ordering of our households, and the responsibilities we have to train others in the righteous life.

Third, inasmuch as Proverbs is moral and formational, it is also developmental, depicting phases of faith formation. The entirety of the book presents progress to wisdom as a journey. The book begins with household instruction of a father (and mother) to his son as young and naive (1:8-9:18) and ends with a mother's instruction to his son as ruler and king (31:1-31). The overall movement of the book of Proverbs is from home to royal court, family to cosmos, boyhood to manhood, naive existence to noble vocation, passive living to proactive leadership. It helps one think about his own progress from child to adult, son to father, student to teacher, apprentice to master, citizen to leader.

A fourth characteristic is important to note: Proverbs highlights the importance of alignment of inner world and outer living. One way to understand Proverbs is as a manual for living wisely in God's world. Wisdom as prudent behavior will only take one so far. Soon, one learns that Proverbs is concerned that we order the world of our inner person so that we can faithfully live in the world that God has made. Many of the Proverbs address internal realities (i.e., motivations, values, love, contentment) and character attributes (i.e., self-control, humility, generosity, patience, etc.) alongside of external conduct (i.e., just scales, prudent speech, diligent work, etc.). The supreme virtue that organizes all other aspects of wisdom and spirituality is the fear of the Lord. This inward disposition of reverence, awe, trust, and submission to God is the kernel from which a life of wisdom blooms.

Although it is ancient in origin, Proverbs is timeless in its relevance. For those looking for specific and anecdotal assistance in daily living, one will encounter teeming waters. For those looking to mature and develop, this book will offer compelling portraits of godly men and godly women (and foils of their opposites). For leaders in home, church, workplace, school, or city, Proverbs assists these overseers, shepherds, and governors to steward their responsibility well. For everyone concerned about faith formation, spiritual growth, and the development of Christian character, this collection of proverbial thinking will give blueprints for how people change. For the young and immature, this book offers a hopeful map for the best of all kinds of lives. For all who want to live prudently before God, shrewdly in the world, and boldly before the watching world, this book commends the best of all paths in the fear of God—a path that requires us to view faith formation and moral development as a journey.

## Key Ideas

- Biblical wisdom involves moral formation in the fear of the Lord.
- The assorted, topical wisdom sayings in Proverbs are undergirded by a unified vision of faith formation that amount to a spiritual pedagogy: a theology of how people change and grow in wisdom.
- In general terms, Proverbs moves from the household to the royal court, depicting faith formation in the family as an incubation chamber for noble vocation in the world.
- Those who are truly wise live faithfully in God's world from their internal world being rightly aligned with God.

## Reflection Questions

<Question id="Pro-Ses3-RefQue-1">1. How do you tend think about the book of Proverbs? What role has it had in your own faith development and spiritual formation?</Question>
<Question id="Pro-Ses3-RefQue-2">2. What have you learned about the importance of the book of Proverbs? What new insights have you gained about why God gave his people this book?</Question>
<Question id="Pro-Ses3-RefQue-3">3. How might Proverbs be relevant to your own faith journey? How might it help you in the leadership and ministry roles in which God has placed you (in your family, church, workplace, and world)?</Question>
